Part IV: Discrete-Time Dynamic Models in Macroeconomics

kapitaali.com
April 14, 2026

Connects to: Principles Ch. 11 (consumption), Ch. 25 (OLG), Ch. 27 (RBC)

Most policy models, DSGE models, and estimation exercises operate in discrete time. The reasons are practical: macroeconomic data arrive at quarterly or monthly intervals; calibration targets are sample moments computed from those data; and the numerical algorithms used for estimation — particle filters, MCMC samplers, value function iteration on finite grids — are inherently discrete.

This part develops the discrete-time parallel to Part III. Where Part III deployed differential equations, phase planes, and Pontryagin’s maximum principle, this part uses difference equations, dynamic programming, and Bellman’s principle of optimality. Every result has a direct continuous-time analogue; spotting the correspondence — eat↔λte^{at} \leftrightarrow \lambda^teat↔λt, stability condition a<0a < 0a<0 ↔\leftrightarrow↔ ∣λ∣<1|\lambda| < 1∣λ∣<1, the Hamiltonian ↔\leftrightarrow↔ the Bellman equation — is the intellectual thread connecting the two parts.

Chapter 14 develops the theory of difference equations systematically, solving the cobweb model and the Samuelson multiplier–accelerator in closed form, and deriving the full stability diagram in parameter space. Chapter 15 builds dynamic programming from the ground up — the Bellman equation, the contraction mapping theorem, value function iteration (VFI), and the Howard policy improvement algorithm — applying them to the buffer-stock consumption model. Chapter 16 solves the Diamond (1965) OLG model in discrete time, deriving dynamic efficiency conditions and analyzing PAYG social security. Chapter 17 assembles the full stochastic RBC model as a recursive competitive equilibrium and solves it via VFI over the (k,A)(k, A)(k,A) state space, computing the second moments used for calibration evaluation.

These four chapters are the computational foundation of Part VII. The reader who understands VFI, the Blanchard–Kahn counting rule, and the recursive competitive equilibrium definition has the tools to understand every step of the DSGE pipeline.

Chapter 14: Difference Equations in Macroeconomics¶

The Cobweb Model and Inventory Cycles

“In discrete time, every model is an iterated map. The question is whether that map converges, oscillates, or explodes — and the eigenvalues of the linearized system give the answer.”

Cross-reference: Principles Ch. 6 (time-series properties of macro data); Ch. 17 (goods market, inventory adjustment model) [P:Ch.6, P:Ch.17]

14.1 Motivating Examples: Why Difference Equations Arise in Macroeconomics¶

Three canonical macroeconomic models generate difference equations naturally.

The inventory adjustment model [P:Ch.17.1]: firms target an inventory stock N∗=νYdN^* = \nu Y^dN∗=νYd proportional to expected demand. If actual inventories Nt−1N_{t-1}Nt−1​ differ from the target, firms partially adjust: ΔYts=β(N∗−Nt−1)\Delta Y_t^s = \beta(N^* - N_{t-1})ΔYts​=β(N∗−Nt−1​), β∈(0,1)\beta \in (0,1)β∈(0,1). With output determining income and demand: Yt=μAˉ−βν(1−b)Yt−1Y_t = \mu \bar{A} - \beta\nu(1-b)Y_{t-1}Yt​=μAˉ−βν(1−b)Yt−1​, a first-order linear difference equation.

The cobweb model: agricultural supply decisions take one period to implement. Farmers plant based on last period’s price; consumers buy at the current clearing price. The resulting price dynamics: Pt+1=−(S′/D′)Pt+constP_{t+1} = -(S'/D')P_t + \text{const}Pt+1​=−(S′/D′)Pt​+const, where S′>0S' > 0S′>0 and D′<0D' < 0D′<0 are supply and demand slopes.

The multiplier–accelerator [P:Ch.8]: Samuelson’s (1939) model combines the Keynesian income multiplier with an investment accelerator, generating a second-order difference equation that can produce oscillatory business cycles.

These three models span the key structural features of macroeconomic difference equations: first-order monotone dynamics, first-order oscillatory dynamics (cobweb with ∣S′/D′∣>1|S'/D'| > 1∣S′/D′∣>1), and second-order complex dynamics (multiplier-accelerator with complex eigenvalues). The theory developed below characterizes all three.

14.2 First-Order Linear Difference Equations: Complete Solution¶

Definition 14.1 (First-Order Linear Difference Equation). A first-order linear difference equation has the form:

xt+1=axt+b,t=0,1,2,…x_{t+1} = ax_t + b, \quad t = 0, 1, 2, \ldotsxt+1​=axt​+b,t=0,1,2,…
(1)

with given initial condition x0x_0x0​.

14.2.1 Homogeneous Solution¶

For b=0b = 0b=0: xt+1=axtx_{t+1} = ax_txt+1​=axt​ has solution xt=atx0x_t = a^t x_0xt​=atx0​.

Stability: xt→0x_t \to 0xt​→0 iff ∣a∣<1|a| < 1∣a∣<1; xtx_txt​ diverges iff ∣a∣>1|a| > 1∣a∣>1; xtx_txt​ cycles between ±x0\pm x_0±x0​ iff a=−1a = -1a=−1; xt=x0x_t = x_0xt​=x0​ for all ttt iff a=1a = 1a=1.

14.2.2 Particular Solution and General Solution¶

For a≠1a \neq 1a=1: the steady state is x∗=b/(1−a)x^* = b/(1-a)x∗=b/(1−a). The general solution:

xt=at(x0−x∗)+x∗,x∗=b1−a.\boxed{x_t = a^t(x_0 - x^*) + x^*, \quad x^* = \frac{b}{1-a}.}xt​=at(x0​−x∗)+x∗,x∗=1−ab​.​
(2)

The term at(x0−x∗)a^t(x_0 - x^*)at(x0​−x∗) is the transient (decays iff ∣a∣<1|a| < 1∣a∣<1); x∗x^*x∗ is the steady state (particular solution).

Convergence:

ConditionBehavior
0<a<10 < a < 10<a<1Monotone convergence to x∗x^*x∗
−1<a<0-1 < a < 0−1<a<0Oscillatory convergence (alternating signs) to x∗x^*x∗
a>1a > 1a>1Monotone divergence
a<−1a < -1a<−1Oscillatory divergence
a=1a = 1a=1No finite steady state; xt=x0+btx_t = x_0 + btxt​=x0​+bt (drift)
a=−1a = -1a=−1Oscillation between x0x_0x0​ and b−x0b - x_0b−x0​

14.2.3 The Cobweb Model: First-Order Dynamics¶

In the cobweb model, supply is based on last period’s price: Qts=α+βPt−1Q^s_t = \alpha + \beta P_{t-1}Qts​=α+βPt−1​, β>0\beta > 0β>0. Demand: Qtd=γ−δPtQ^d_t = \gamma - \delta P_tQtd​=γ−δPt​, δ>0\delta > 0δ>0. Market clearing Qts=QtdQ^s_t = Q^d_tQts​=Qtd​:

Pt=γ−αδ−βδPt−1.P_t = \frac{\gamma - \alpha}{\delta} - \frac{\beta}{\delta}P_{t-1}.Pt​=δγ−α​−δβ​Pt−1​.
(3)

This is a first-order difference equation with a=−β/δa = -\beta/\deltaa=−β/δ and b=(γ−α)/δb = (\gamma-\alpha)/\deltab=(γ−α)/δ. Stability requires ∣a∣<1|a| < 1∣a∣<1, i.e., β<δ\beta < \deltaβ<δ: supply must be more inelastic than demand.

Rational expectations correction: If farmers correctly anticipate the equilibrium price Pte=P∗=b/(1+β/δ)P_t^e = P^* = b/(1+\beta/\delta)Pte​=P∗=b/(1+β/δ) for all ttt, there are no cobweb dynamics — markets clear immediately at the steady state. The cobweb arises only under naive expectations (Pte=Pt−1P^e_t = P_{t-1}Pte​=Pt−1​). This motivates the rational expectations assumption: if agents understand the model, they eliminate self-fulfilling oscillations [P:Ch.16].

14.3 Second-Order Linear Difference Equations¶

Definition 14.2 (Second-Order Linear Difference Equation). A second-order linear difference equation has the form:

xt+2+pxt+1+qxt=c,x_{t+2} + px_{t+1} + qx_t = c,xt+2​+pxt+1​+qxt​=c,
(4)

with initial conditions x0x_0x0​ and x1x_1x1​. The characteristic equation is:

λ2+pλ+q=0,λ1,2=−p±p2−4q2.\lambda^2 + p\lambda + q = 0, \quad \lambda_{1,2} = \frac{-p \pm \sqrt{p^2 - 4q}}{2}.λ2+pλ+q=0,λ1,2​=2−p±p2−4q​​.
(5)

Theorem 14.1 (General Solution — Second-Order). Let λ1,λ2\lambda_1, \lambda_2λ1​,λ2​ be the roots of the characteristic equation and x∗=c/(1+p+q)x^* = c/(1+p+q)x∗=c/(1+p+q) (assuming 1+p+q≠01+p+q \neq 01+p+q=0).

Case 1: Distinct real roots (p2>4qp^2 > 4qp2>4q).

xt=C1λ1t+C2λ2t+x∗.x_t = C_1\lambda_1^t + C_2\lambda_2^t + x^*.xt​=C1​λ1t​+C2​λ2t​+x∗.
(6)

Case 2: Repeated root (p2=4qp^2 = 4qp2=4q, λ1=λ2=λ\lambda_1 = \lambda_2 = \lambdaλ1​=λ2​=λ).

xt=(C1+C2t)λt+x∗.x_t = (C_1 + C_2 t)\lambda^t + x^*.xt​=(C1​+C2​t)λt+x∗.
(7)

Case 3: Complex conjugate roots (p2<4qp^2 < 4qp2<4q), λ1,2=re±iθ\lambda_{1,2} = r e^{\pm i\theta}λ1,2​=re±iθ.

xt=rt(C1cos⁡θt+C2sin⁡θt)+x∗,x_t = r^t(C_1\cos\theta t + C_2\sin\theta t) + x^*,xt​=rt(C1​cosθt+C2​sinθt)+x∗,
(8)

where r=qr = \sqrt{q}r=q​ and θ=arctan⁡(4q−p2/(−p))∈(0,π)\theta = \arctan\left(\sqrt{4q-p^2}/(-p)\right) \in (0,\pi)θ=arctan(4q−p2​/(−p))∈(0,π).

Proof of Case 3. Write λ=r(cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ)\lambda = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)λ=r(cosθ+isinθ) and λˉ=r(cos⁡θ−isin⁡θ)\bar\lambda = r(\cos\theta - i\sin\theta)λˉ=r(cosθ−isinθ). Then λt=rteiθt=rt(cos⁡θt+isin⁡θt)\lambda^t = r^t e^{i\theta t} = r^t(\cos\theta t + i\sin\theta t)λt=rteiθt=rt(cosθt+isinθt), and the real general solution combines λt\lambda^tλt and λˉt\bar\lambda^tλˉt with conjugate coefficients, giving the stated form. □\square□

Stability for second-order equations: The system is stable (both roots with ∣λ∣<1|\lambda| < 1∣λ∣<1) iff:

∣p∣<1+qandq<1.|p| < 1 + q \quad \text{and} \quad q < 1.∣p∣<1+qandq<1.
(9)

These are necessary and sufficient. For complex roots (r=qr = \sqrt{q}r=q​), stability reduces to r<1r < 1r<1, i.e., q<1q < 1q<1.

14.4 The Multiplier–Accelerator: Second-Order Dynamics in Full¶

Definition 14.3 (Samuelson Multiplier–Accelerator). Samuelson’s (1939) model:

Ct=bYt−1,It=v(Ct−Ct−1),Yt=Ct+It+G.C_t = bY_{t-1}, \quad I_t = v(C_t - C_{t-1}), \quad Y_t = C_t + I_t + G.Ct​=bYt−1​,It​=v(Ct​−Ct−1​),Yt​=Ct​+It​+G.
(10)

Substituting: Yt=b(1+v)Yt−1−bvYt−2+GY_t = b(1+v)Y_{t-1} - bvY_{t-2} + GYt​=b(1+v)Yt−1​−bvYt−2​+G, or:

Yt+2−b(1+v)Yt+1+bv⋅Yt=G.Y_{t+2} - b(1+v)Y_{t+1} + bv\cdot Y_t = G.Yt+2​−b(1+v)Yt+1​+bv⋅Yt​=G.
(11)

This is a second-order difference equation with p=−b(1+v)p = -b(1+v)p=−b(1+v) and q=bvq = bvq=bv. The steady state Y∗=G/(1−b)Y^* = G/(1-b)Y∗=G/(1−b).

Characteristic equation: λ2−b(1+v)λ+bv=0\lambda^2 - b(1+v)\lambda + bv = 0λ2−b(1+v)λ+bv=0.

Discriminant: Δ=b2(1+v)2−4bv=b2(1−v)2+2bv(b−2)\Delta = b^2(1+v)^2 - 4bv = b^2(1-v)^2 + 2bv(b-2)Δ=b2(1+v)2−4bv=b2(1−v)2+2bv(b−2)... Let me compute directly: Δ=[b(1+v)]2−4bv=b2+2bv+b2v2−4bv=b2(1−v)2+2b(bv−2v)=b2(1+v)2−4bv\Delta = [b(1+v)]^2 - 4bv = b^2 + 2bv + b^2v^2 - 4bv = b^2(1-v)^2 + 2b(bv-2v) = b^2(1+v)^2 - 4bvΔ=[b(1+v)]2−4bv=b2+2bv+b2v2−4bv=b2(1−v)2+2b(bv−2v)=b2(1+v)2−4bv.

Case analysis for business cycle character:

RegionEigenvalue typeDynamic path
b2(1+v)2>4bvb^2(1+v)^2 > 4bvb2(1+v)2>4bvTwo distinct realMonotone approach
b2(1+v)2<4bvb^2(1+v)^2 < 4bvb2(1+v)2<4bvComplex conjugatesOscillatory (cyclical)
bv<1bv < 1bv<1r=bv<1r = \sqrt{bv} < 1r=bv​<1Convergent (dampened) cycles
bv=1bv = 1bv=1r=1r = 1r=1Neutral oscillation (limit cycle)
bv>1bv > 1bv>1r>1r > 1r>1Explosive oscillation

Theorem 14.2 (Stability Conditions for Multiplier–Accelerator). The Samuelson multiplier-accelerator is stable iff bv<1bv < 1bv<1, and generates business cycles (oscillatory path) iff b2(1+v)2<4bvb^2(1+v)^2 < 4bvb2(1+v)2<4bv.

Proof. Stability requires q=bv<1q = bv < 1q=bv<1 (necessary and sufficient for the complex-root modulus to be less than 1). Oscillation requires p2<4qp^2 < 4qp2<4q, i.e., b2(1+v)2<4bvb^2(1+v)^2 < 4bvb2(1+v)2<4bv. □\square□

The period of oscillation: For complex roots with modulus rrr and argument θ\thetaθ, the period of one oscillation is T=2π/θT = 2\pi/\thetaT=2π/θ periods. With b=0.8b = 0.8b=0.8 and v=0.9v = 0.9v=0.9: r=0.72=0.849r = \sqrt{0.72} = 0.849r=0.72​=0.849, θ=arccos⁡(−b(1+v)/(2r))=arccos⁡(−0.72/(0.849×2×1.9))≈arccos⁡(−0.224)≈1.796\theta = \arccos(-b(1+v)/(2r)) = \arccos(-0.72/(0.849\times2\times1.9)) ≈ \arccos(-0.224) ≈ 1.796θ=arccos(−b(1+v)/(2r))=arccos(−0.72/(0.849×2×1.9))≈arccos(−0.224)≈1.796 radians, period ≈2π/1.796≈3.5\approx 2\pi/1.796 \approx 3.5≈2π/1.796≈3.5 periods — a business cycle of roughly 3–4 years for quarterly data.

14.5 Systems of Linear Difference Equations¶

Definition 14.4 (State-Space Form). A system of nnn first-order linear difference equations:

xt+1=Axt+But,x0 given,\mathbf{x}_{t+1} = A\mathbf{x}_t + B\mathbf{u}_t, \quad \mathbf{x}_0 \text{ given},xt+1​=Axt​+But​,x0​ given,
(12)

where xt∈Rn\mathbf{x}_t \in \mathbb{R}^nxt​∈Rn is the state vector, ut∈Rm\mathbf{u}_t \in \mathbb{R}^mut​∈Rm is an exogenous input, A∈Rn×nA \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}A∈Rn×n is the transition matrix, and B∈Rn×mB \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times m}B∈Rn×m is the input matrix.

Theorem 14.3 (Solution of Linear State-Space System). The solution of xt+1=Axt\mathbf{x}_{t+1} = A\mathbf{x}_txt+1​=Axt​ is:

xt=Atx0=PDtP−1x0,\mathbf{x}_t = A^t\mathbf{x}_0 = PD^tP^{-1}\mathbf{x}_0,xt​=Atx0​=PDtP−1x0​,
(13)

where A=PDP−1A = PDP^{-1}A=PDP−1 is the eigendecomposition. The general solution with inputs is:

xt=Atx0+∑j=0t−1At−1−jBuj.\mathbf{x}_t = A^t\mathbf{x}_0 + \sum_{j=0}^{t-1}A^{t-1-j}B\mathbf{u}_j.xt​=Atx0​+j=0∑t−1​At−1−jBuj​.
(14)

Stability: The system is stable iff all eigenvalues of AAA satisfy ∣λi∣<1|\lambda_i| < 1∣λi​∣<1.

Impulse response: The response at horizon hhh to a unit shock u0=ej\mathbf{u}_0 = \mathbf{e}_ju0​=ej​ is Ah−1Bej=Ah−1BjA^{h-1}B\mathbf{e}_j = A^{h-1}B_jAh−1Bej​=Ah−1Bj​ (the jjj-th column of Ah−1BA^{h-1}BAh−1B). The full IRF sequence {Bj,ABj,A2Bj,…}\{B_j, AB_j, A^2B_j, \ldots\}{Bj​,ABj​,A2Bj​,…} decays to zero iff all ∣λi(A)∣<1|\lambda_i(A)| < 1∣λi​(A)∣<1.

In APL, the IRF at all horizons 0..H-1 is generated in one expression:

14.6 Worked Example: Full Solution of the Multiplier–Accelerator¶

Setup: b=0.8b = 0.8b=0.8, v=0.8v = 0.8v=0.8, G=100G = 100G=100.

Steady state: Y∗=G/(1−b)=100/0.2=500Y^* = G/(1-b) = 100/0.2 = 500Y∗=G/(1−b)=100/0.2=500.

Characteristic equation: λ2−0.8(1.8)λ+0.8×0.8=λ2−1.44λ+0.64=0\lambda^2 - 0.8(1.8)\lambda + 0.8\times0.8 = \lambda^2 - 1.44\lambda + 0.64 = 0λ2−0.8(1.8)λ+0.8×0.8=λ2−1.44λ+0.64=0.

Roots: λ=(1.44±1.442−4×0.64)/2=(1.44±2.0736−2.56)/2\lambda = (1.44 \pm \sqrt{1.44^2 - 4\times0.64})/2 = (1.44 \pm \sqrt{2.0736 - 2.56})/2λ=(1.44±1.442−4×0.64​)/2=(1.44±2.0736−2.56​)/2.

Discriminant: 2.0736−2.56=−0.4864<02.0736 - 2.56 = -0.4864 < 02.0736−2.56=−0.4864<0 → complex roots.

r=q=0.64=0.8r = \sqrt{q} = \sqrt{0.64} = 0.8r=q​=0.64​=0.8, θ=arccos⁡(−p/(2r))=arccos⁡(1.44/(2×0.8))=arccos⁡(0.9)≈0.4510\theta = \arccos(-p/(2r)) = \arccos(1.44/(2\times0.8)) = \arccos(0.9) \approx 0.4510θ=arccos(−p/(2r))=arccos(1.44/(2×0.8))=arccos(0.9)≈0.4510 radians.

Period: 2π/0.4510≈13.92\pi/0.4510 \approx 13.92π/0.4510≈13.9 periods.

General solution:

Yt=500+0.8t(C1cos⁡(0.451t)+C2sin⁡(0.451t)).Y_t = 500 + 0.8^t(C_1\cos(0.451t) + C_2\sin(0.451t)).Yt​=500+0.8t(C1​cos(0.451t)+C2​sin(0.451t)).
(15)

Initial conditions: Y0=480Y_0 = 480Y0​=480 (4% below steady state), Y1=490Y_1 = 490Y1​=490 (2% below).

From Y0=500+C1=480Y_0 = 500 + C_1 = 480Y0​=500+C1​=480: C1=−20C_1 = -20C1​=−20.

From Y1=500+0.8(C1cos⁡0.451+C2sin⁡0.451)=490Y_1 = 500 + 0.8(C_1\cos0.451 + C_2\sin0.451) = 490Y1​=500+0.8(C1​cos0.451+C2​sin0.451)=490: 0.8(−20×0.900+C2×0.436)=−10⇒−14.4+0.349C2=−10⇒C2=4.4/0.349=12.60.8(-20\times0.900 + C_2\times0.436) = -10 \Rightarrow -14.4 + 0.349C_2 = -10 \Rightarrow C_2 = 4.4/0.349 = 12.60.8(−20×0.900+C2​×0.436)=−10⇒−14.4+0.349C2​=−10⇒C2​=4.4/0.349=12.6.

⍝ osc_stable                  → dampened oscillation (business cycles)
⍝ ~stable_mat ∧ complex_mat  → explosive oscillation
⍝ ~stable_mat ∧ ~complex_mat → monotone divergence
import numpy as np; import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.colors import ListedColormap

b_vals = np.linspace(0.01, 0.99, 200)
v_vals = np.linspace(0.01, 2.99, 200)
B, V = np.meshgrid(b_vals, v_vals)

stable   = B*V < 1
complex_ = B**2*(1+V)**2 < 4*B*V

region = np.zeros_like(B, dtype=int)
region[stable & ~complex_]  = 1  # monotone convergence
region[stable & complex_]   = 2  # oscillatory convergence (cycles)
region[~stable & complex_]  = 3  # explosive oscillation
region[~stable & ~complex_] = 4  # monotone divergence

cmap = ListedColormap(['white','lightblue','steelblue','tomato','salmon'])
plt.figure(figsize=(8,6))
plt.contourf(B, V, region, levels=[-0.5,0.5,1.5,2.5,3.5,4.5], cmap=cmap)
plt.contour(B, V, stable.astype(int), levels=[0.5], colors='black', linewidths=2)
plt.xlabel('MPC (b)'); plt.ylabel('Accelerator (v)')
plt.title('Stability diagram: multiplier-accelerator\n(dark blue = oscillatory convergence = business cycles)')
plt.colorbar(ticks=[0,1,2,3,4], label='Region')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

# Time path simulation
b, v, G = 0.8, 0.8, 100
Y = np.zeros(80); Y[0], Y[1] = 480, 490
for t in range(2, 80):
    Y[t] = b*(1+v)*Y[t-1] - b*v*Y[t-2] + G
plt.figure(); plt.plot(Y); plt.axhline(G/(1-b), c='r', ls='--', label='Y*=500')
plt.xlabel('Period'); plt.ylabel('Output'); plt.title('Multiplier-Accelerator Path (b=0.8, v=0.8)'); plt.legend(); plt.show()
b, v, G = 0.8, 0.8, 100.0
Ystar = G / (1-b)

# Characteristic roots
p_coef, q_coef = -b*(1+v), b*v
disc = p_coef^2 - 4*q_coef
if disc < 0
    r = sqrt(q_coef); theta = acos(-p_coef/(2r))
    println("Complex roots: r=$(round(r,digits=3)), θ=$(round(theta,digits=3)), period=$(round(2π/theta,digits=1))")
else
    lam = [(-p_coef + sqrt(disc))/2, (-p_coef - sqrt(disc))/2]
    println("Real roots: λ₁=$(round(lam[1],digits=3)), λ₂=$(round(lam[2],digits=3))")
end

Y = zeros(80); Y[1], Y[2] = 480.0, 490.0
for t in 3:80
    Y[t] = b*(1+v)*Y[t-1] - b*v*Y[t-2] + G
end
println("Y[1]=$(Y[1]), Y[40]=$(round(Y[40],digits=1)), Y[80]=$(round(Y[80],digits=1)), Y*=$(Ystar)")
b <- 0.8; v <- 0.8; G <- 100
Ystar <- G/(1-b)
Y <- numeric(80); Y[1] <- 480; Y[2] <- 490
for(t in 3:80) Y[t] <- b*(1+v)*Y[t-1] - b*v*Y[t-2] + G
cat(sprintf("Steady state: %.0f; Y[40]=%.1f; Y[80]=%.1f\n", Ystar, Y[40], Y[80]))
# Period of oscillation
disc <- (b*(1+v))^2 - 4*b*v
if(disc < 0) {
  r <- sqrt(b*v); theta <- acos(b*(1+v)/(2*r))
  cat(sprintf("Period ≈ %.1f quarters\n", 2*pi/theta))
}
plot(Y, type='l', xlab='Period', ylab='Output', main='Multiplier-Accelerator')
abline(h=Ystar, lty=2, col='red')

14.8 Chapter Summary¶

Key results:

  • First-order equations xt+1=axt+bx_{t+1} = ax_t + bxt+1​=axt​+b have steady state x∗=b/(1−a)x^* = b/(1-a)x∗=b/(1−a) and general solution xt=at(x0−x∗)+x∗x_t = a^t(x_0-x^*)+x^*xt​=at(x0​−x∗)+x∗; stable iff ∣a∣<1|a| < 1∣a∣<1.

  • The cobweb model is a first-order equation with a=−β/δa = -\beta/\deltaa=−β/δ; stable iff supply is more inelastic than demand (β<δ\beta < \deltaβ<δ); rational expectations eliminate cobweb dynamics entirely.

  • Second-order equations xt+2+pxt+1+qxt=cx_{t+2}+px_{t+1}+qx_t = cxt+2​+pxt+1​+qxt​=c have solutions characterized by their characteristic roots — real monotone, complex oscillatory, or explosive — with stability requiring ∣p∣<1+q|p| < 1+q∣p∣<1+q and q<1q < 1q<1.

  • The multiplier–accelerator Yt=b(1+v)Yt−1−bvYt−2+GY_t = b(1+v)Y_{t-1} - bvY_{t-2} + GYt​=b(1+v)Yt−1​−bvYt−2​+G is stable iff bv<1bv < 1bv<1 and oscillatory (business cycles) iff b2(1+v)2<4bvb^2(1+v)^2 < 4bvb2(1+v)2<4bv; the oscillation period is 2π/arccos⁡[−b(1+v)/(2bv)]2\pi/\arccos[-b(1+v)/(2\sqrt{bv})]2π/arccos[−b(1+v)/(2bv​)].

  • State-space form xt+1=Axt\mathbf{x}_{t+1} = A\mathbf{x}_txt+1​=Axt​: stable iff all eigenvalues of AAA satisfy ∣λi∣<1|\lambda_i| < 1∣λi​∣<1; IRFs are AhA^hAh applied to the shock vector.

  • In APL: simulation is a scan step \ T ⍴ ⊂ initial_state; IRFs are {(A⍣⍵)+.×B}¨⍳H; the stability diagram is b_grid ∘.{⍺×⍵ < 1} v_grid.
